title: Japanese terms and dojo etiquette
note: Japanese arts share a vocabulary. Do means a way of life and training, jutsu a technique or method; budo is the martial way. Etiquette, or reigi, shapes the dojo: bow on entering and leaving, bow to partners before and after practice, respect seniors, and keep the mat and uniform clean.

read.title: Way and technique
text: Many Japanese art names end in do or jutsu, and the difference carries a philosophy. Jutsu means technique or method, as in jujutsu, the old grappling arts of the samurai. Do means a way, a path followed for life. When Jigoro Kano turned jujutsu into judo, he signaled that training should build character as well as skill. The broader idea is budo, the martial way.

Etiquette, called reigi, makes that idea visible. Students bow, rei, when they enter or leave the dojo, literally the place of the way, and when they step on or off the tatami. They bow to partners before and after practice, often saying onegaishimasu, please train with me, and afterward arigato gozaimashita, thank you. Seniors, senpai, look after juniors, kohai, and everyone addresses the teacher as sensei, one born before.
Two mental ideals often appear in classes. Zanshin, remaining mind, is alertness that continues after a technique ends. Mushin, no-mind, is action that flows without hesitation.
